findings.finding: C2 requires a fold to be 'reachable on the sync remote's tickets ref ≥ N days', and S1 says this is computed from 'pure git reachability + timestamps'. Git records no push or arrival time on a remote. Commit timestamps are client-authored, and remote reflogs are unavailable on GitHub and S3. The source of the '≥ N days on remote' clock is therefore unstated.
scenarios: A clone with a skewed clock authors a SNAPSHOT commit dated 31 days ago that was pushed yesterday. It is treated as eligible, and in-horizon clones lose state.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a 'Failure-disposition contract' section stating, per arm (S3 lock failure/partial swap, CAS retry exhaustion, stale-clone override), whether it is retryable or fatal/NEEDS_INVESTIGATION and what the operator/client surfaces.
evidence: "write ONE rewritten bundle and delete the originals"
"else abort+retry"

findings.finding: The plan adds several failure arms without stating their disposition. (a) S3 exclusive replacement: lock-acquisition failure, or a crash between 'write ONE rewritten bundle' and 'delete the originals'. That partial state leaves both heads present, which the auto-doctor would merge, and the plan does not say whether this surfaces as fatal/NEEDS_INVESTIGATION or auto-restores from the rollback prefix. (b) The CAS 'abort+retry' arm has no retry budget, and the disposition when retries are exhausted is unstated. (c) The stale-clone forced override discards divergent work, but the plan does not say what the user or caller sees: a fatal error requiring acknowledgment, a warning, or a silent reset.
findings.location: Feasibility — S3 bundle-set replacement and 'abort+retry'; Mechanism S3 forced override
scenarios: A crash after the new bundle is written but before the originals are deleted leaves two heads; clients' auto-doctor merges them, causing silent resurrection with no operator-visible failure.
CAS retries loop indefinitely under write load with no terminal disposition.
A drifted clone silently loses local work with no surfaced signal.
findings.suggested_fix: Proposed per-arm dispositions: S3 lock not acquired → retryable (WAIT_AND_RETRY). Partial swap detected (new and old bundles coexist) → fatal NEEDS_INVESTIGATION, auto-restore from the rollback prefix before releasing the lock, never left for the auto-doctor. CAS retries exhausted after K attempts → retryable INDETERMINATE exit, with no state change. Stale-clone override → surface an explicit non-silent warning listing the discarded event files, and preserve them in a local backup ref.

The ADR 0031 precedent the plan cites CASes the unprotected custom ref `refs/reconciler/lock`, not a protected branch, so it does not show the capability. findings.finding: Re-anchoring enforce_since cannot be atomic with the tickets swap, and the plan gives no cross-branch ordering. It says 'the same S2 pass ... re-anchors enforce_since to the baseline', but enforce_since is pinned to a tickets commit SHA in rebar.toml on main, a separately reviewed branch. Once the tickets ref is swapped, that pinned SHA is no longer on the branch CI fetches (CI fetches only '+tickets'; the backup ref is not fetched), until a main change moving the anchor is reviewed and merged. During that window every verify-identity run on main, and on every open change based on the old rebar.toml, evaluates ancestry against a missing or unrelated anchor. Rolling back needs another main change.

findings.suggested_fix: Before the swap, set the CI env override REBAR_IDENTITY_ENFORCE_SINCE to a stable symbolic ref (e.g. a tag on the tickets remote that the swap moves atomically along with the branch, fetched by CI). The anchor then flips in the same atomic push and rolls back with it, and rebar.toml is changed to that ref name afterward.

"~14K commits/day"
"a changed head set aborts+retries"
findings.finding: The plan has no hold-open window: the rewrite runs offline, then publishes via CAS 'iff remote unchanged since T0, else abort+retry'. At the measured ~14K commits/day (~one push every 6s), any rewrite and upload taking longer than a few seconds will almost always lose the CAS. Convergence (liveness) of the retry loop is asserted, not measured. No incremental-catch-up or brief-quiesce strategy is validated.
findings.location: Feasibility — 'replace published history iff remote unchanged since T0, else abort+retry'; Measured '~14K commits/day'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the swap converge under continuous writes: specify an incremental catch-up loop that grafts the T0→Tn delta onto the existing baseline and re-leases on Tn, with a bounded retry count and an explicit fallback such as a short write-quiesce window.
evidence: Plan: 'replace published history iff remote unchanged since T0, else abort+retry'; 'no clone registry, no hold-open window'
Plan: '~14K commits/day'
reclaim_publish.py:53: 'The remote moved since T0. Nothing was written; recompute the reclaim and retry.'
findings.finding: The publish-swap CAS will livelock in practice. It is a pure 'replace iff remote unchanged since T0, else abort+retry' with 'no hold-open window'. The plan itself measures ~14K commits/day (about 10 per minute) on tickets. Between T0 and the push, S2 must run fast-import over 235K commits, re-sign the baseline, fsck, replay the full log and run verify-authorship (which takes tens of minutes on its own), so the remote will almost certainly have moved. If every retry recomputes from scratch, the lease will essentially never hold. The plan names no incremental catch-up that re-parents the T0→T1 delta onto the already-built baseline and re-leases on T1, and no bounded write-quiesce for the final step.
scenarios: An operator starts a reclaim. By the time verification finishes, about a hundred new ticket commits have landed, the lease fails, and every recompute-and-retry cycle fails the same way.
S3 backend: the bundle head set changes on every auto-push, so the set-equality precondition never holds.
findings.suggested_fix: Because in-horizon commits are kept above the baseline, re-parent only the new delta (old_tip..current_remote) onto the rewritten tip with fast-import, re-verify just that delta, and retry the lease against the new tip. Repeat until the lease succeeds, up to K attempts, then fall back to a brief, explicit write pause for the final push.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the S3 swap crash-safe: have the auto-doctor refuse to fold any head that a published superseding epoch has replaced (or detect a reclaim-in-progress marker), and verify that the helper's lock lease covers the full-history bundle upload or is renewed during it.
evidence: Plan: 'back up the bundle set to a rollback prefix, write ONE rewritten bundle and delete the originals — deliberately BYPASSING the auto-doctor'
reclaim_publish.py:221-226: put_bundle(new_key) and then a loop of delete_object over the originals, with no recovery marker
s3_doctor.py:3: 'Fold all heads into the published ref under the write lock' — the doctor merges any multi-bundle state
findings.finding: The S3 'exclusive bundle-set replacement' is not atomic, and a partial failure brings back the very hazard it exists to avoid. The sequence is: write ONE rewritten bundle, then delete the originals. A crash, a network error, or the per-ref lock expiring or being broken between the put and the deletes leaves the ref advertising old and new heads together. The next client sync then runs the non-interactive auto-doctor, which merges every head losslessly. That reattaches the old history, which the plan itself calls 'MERGED BACK (resurrected)'. The plan also does not check that the git-remote-s3 lock outlives a full-history bundle upload.
scenarios: The operator's process dies after uploading the new bundle but before deleting the originals; the next client auto-sync sees two heads and the doctor merges the old history back in.
A long upload of a large full-history bundle outlives the helper's lock, a client push takes the lock, and a third head appears.
findings.suggested_fix: Before any write, place a reclaim marker object that names the new tip and the superseded heads. Teach s3_doctor to drop superseded heads instead of merging them when the marker or a superseding epoch is present. Finish or roll back idempotently from the marker on retry.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the S3 swap's crash/partial-failure protocol: a write-ahead marker (or manifest) recording the intended final head set, a resume rule that is idempotent (re-run completes or rolls back the deletes), behavior when the lock expires partway, and a guarantee that the auto-doctor stays suppressed while more than one head exists mid-swap.
evidence: "back up the bundle set to a rollback prefix, write ONE rewritten bundle and delete the originals — deliberately BYPASSING the auto-doctor"
"its non-interactive auto-doctor (`s3_doctor.py`) folds divergent heads by lossless merge and NEVER discards a head, so a normally-pushed rewrite would be MERGED BACK (resurrected)"
The plan says nothing about crash or lock-expiry mid-replacement, a write-ahead marker, or a resume/idempotency protocol.
findings.finding: The S3 publish swap has several steps and isn't atomic ('back up the bundle set to a rollback prefix, write ONE rewritten bundle and delete the originals'). The plan doesn't define what happens if it fails partway, how to resume, or whether it's idempotent. If the process crashes, or the per-ref push-lock expires, after the rewritten bundle is written but before every original is deleted, the ref has more than one head. The plan itself says the non-interactive auto-doctor 'folds divergent heads by lossless merge and NEVER discards a head', so it would merge the old history back into the new baseline. That resurrects the reclaimed history and could leave a merged graph where enforce_since and ledger annotations are inconsistent.
scenarios: The process is killed after the new bundle is uploaded and two of five original bundles are deleted. On the next client fetch the auto-doctor sees several heads and merges the old history back in.
The push-lock TTL runs out during a slow bulk delete, and a concurrent client push lands between the deletes.
findings.suggested_fix: Before deleting anything, write a reclaim-intent marker under the ref prefix (new bundle id, original bundle ids, rollback prefix). Have the auto-doctor and fetch path refuse to merge while the marker exists. Make the swap re-runnable: if the marker exists, finish deleting the listed originals, or restore them from the rollback prefix if the new bundle is missing. Remove the marker last. Renew or verify the push-lock before each delete.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify how writes that land after T0 are carried into the swap: rewrite only the history below the horizon once, then, on each retry, replay just the T0..current-tip event files onto the new baseline and retry the CAS against the fresh tip, with a bounded retry count and a fallback (e.g. a brief writer pause) if the CAS keeps losing the race.
evidence: "replace published history iff remote unchanged since T0, else abort+retry"
"no clone registry, no hold-open window"
"~14K commits/day"
"235,482 commits, 408,295 trees"
findings.finding: Writes that land during the migration window are handled only by 'abort+retry' against T0. The plan measures ~14K commits/day (roughly one every 6 seconds), and rewriting 235K commits / 408K trees is not instant. So the remote will almost certainly have moved past T0 by push time, and every retry hits the same race. The plan doesn't say how the post-T0 tail is carried onto the new baseline (re-run the whole rewrite, or cheaply replay only the tail), and it gives no bound on retries. It also rules out a hold-open window ('no hold-open window').
scenarios: The rewrite takes N minutes, dozens of auto-pushes land in the meantime, the CAS fails, a full re-rewrite starts, and it fails again. The swap never publishes.
An operator who is frustrated by repeated aborts falls back to a manual write pause or a forced push without the lease, losing in-flight writes.
findings.suggested_fix: Split S2 into (i) a slow, cacheable rewrite of history below the horizon into a baseline checkpoint and (ii) a fast tail step that replays the event files added since the baseline anchor onto that baseline. Each CAS retry re-runs only step (ii) against the newly observed tip, so the race window is seconds, not the full rewrite time.

evidence: Plan: "under git-remote-s3's per-ref push-lock, enumerate bundles ..., assert the head set == T0 ..., back up the bundle set to a rollback prefix, write ONE rewritten bundle and delete the originals"
docs/s3-backend.md:148-153: "when `acquire_lock` finds the existing lock older than the TTL it deletes it and re-acquires in the same call ... The TTL is `DEFAULT_LOCK_TTL_SECONDS = 60`"
ADR 0093:63-73: the helper self-heals a stale lock once it is older than 60s; overridable only through the env var GIT_REMOTE_S3_LOCK_TTL_SECONDS, which every client reads
src/rebar/_commands/reclaim_publish.py:196-204 takes the lock once and never renews it across the copy, upload and delete steps
Evidence class: Partially-verified (the lock exists; whether it stays exclusive for longer than the TTL is contradicted by the documented stale-clear behaviour)
findings.finding: The S3 adapter claims an 'EXCLUSIVE offline bundle-set replacement' under git-remote-s3's per-ref push-lock, with 'No acknowledged write is lost'. But that lock has a 60s TTL, and the next acquirer deletes and re-takes any lock older than that. The swap backs up every bundle, uploads one rewritten bundle of hundreds of MiB, then deletes the originals, which will normally take longer than 60s. A normal push could then take the lock mid-swap and add a bundle. That bundle would either be deleted along with the originals (if its key was enumerated) or left beside the new bundle as a multi-bundle state, which the auto-doctor would fold back in (resurrecting the old history). The plan does not say how the lock is extended, renewed or fenced for the whole swap.
scenarios: A ~400 MiB rewritten-bundle upload takes 3 minutes; at t=61s another clone's auto-push clears the 'stale' lock and adds a bundle; the swap then deletes originals or leaves 2 bundles, and the next push runs the doctor, which merges the pre-rewrite history back in
findings.suggested_fix: Add a spike to S2: measure swap duration at production bundle size against a real bucket. Then pick one design and state it: (a) re-enumerate bundles right before each delete and abort/roll back if any key not in T0 appears; (b) upload the new bundle and back up the originals before taking the lock, so the locked critical section is only enumerate, assert, delete, init_remote_head and fits well under 60s; or (c) run the swap inside an announced write-quiesce window. Record the measured duration against the TTL.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Replace the `git fast-import --version` preflight with a verified check (e.g. `git version` with a minimum-version comparison, or a tiny real fast-import round-trip in a temp repo), checked against `git fast-import -h` output

Evidence class: Unverified, probable MISMATCH (could not run git --help here; claim based on fast-import's documented option set, which lists no --version)
findings.finding: The plan's portability preflight is `git fast-import --version`, but as far as I know fast-import does not accept `--version`. Its option parser rejects unknown `--` options, and git only handles `--version` at the top level (`git --version` / `git version`). The preflight would probably exit non-zero (or, if it were treated as a stream-reading command, block on stdin) on every git install. That would wrongly fail or hang the preflight. fast-import is also a builtin, so checking that it exists adds nothing beyond checking git's version.
scenarios: The S2 shadow-clone prototype's preflight fails on every machine with 'unknown option --version', blocking the reclaim for no real reason
findings.suggested_fix: Preflight with `git version` (parse it and assert a minimum) and, if needed, a no-op smoke test: `printf 'done\n' | git fast-import --done --quiet` in a scratch `git init --bare` repo, asserting exit 0.

findings.finding: The S3 adapter depends on git-remote-s3 internals that ADR 0093 calls private, with no stable public API: the bundle-key layout `<prefix>/<ref>/<sha>.bundle`, `.s3` raw client calls, `init_remote_head`, and the lock semantics. scenarios: An upstream release changes the bundle naming or lock key; the head-set assertion compares the wrong strings or the delete misses keys, during an irreversible swap
findings.suggested_fix: Have the S3 adapter's preflight read `importlib.metadata.version('git-remote-s3')`, assert it is in a tested range, and refuse the swap otherwise; record the tested version in the S0 ADR.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make S1 eligibility measure remote-reachability duration as C2 states, or record in ADR 0106 that committer age is an accepted proxy and name the late-push case as residual.
evidence: Parent C2: 'that fold reachable on the sync remote's tickets ref ≥ N days'; deferred S1: 'remote-reachable ≥ N days'.

scenarios: A clone that was offline for weeks merges and pushes commits whose committer dates are already older than N days. Those commits become collapse-eligible the moment they reach the remote, even though no other clone has seen them yet.
findings.suggested_fix: Either anchor eligibility to remote-observed evidence (for example, the remote-tracking ref's reflog entry that first contained the commit, or a remote-side timestamped marker), or amend ADR 0106 C2 and e32d's ACs to state the committer-date proxy explicitly with its late-push caveat and why it is safe.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Align the stale definition: either base it on last successful convergence (fetch/merge time) or record the push-failure case as an accepted residual in ADR 0106 §5.
evidence: aff9: 'The clone is *stale* iff its oldest unpushed event's `ts` is older than `now − [reclaim].horizon_days` ... Because every write auto-pushes (I5), the oldest unpushed write bounds the clone's last convergence.'
866f: 'a clone whose last convergence is older than N days overrides local with remote'.
Parent: 'residual loss of a >N-day-drifted clone's divergent work is ACCEPTED'.
findings.finding: aff9 calls a clone stale when its oldest unpushed event is older than N days. That is a proxy for the parent/ADR condition 'a clone whose last convergence is older than N days'. A clone that kept fetching and merging but whose pushes failed for more than N days would be classified stale, and its work discarded, even though it converged recently. That loss goes beyond the accepted '>N-day-drifted clone' residual.
scenarios: A clone whose push credentials expired keeps pulling (so it has converged recently) and accumulates writes for more than N days. After the reclaim swap it is classified stale and all of those unpushed writes are dropped, kept only in a local backup ref.
findings.suggested_fix: Record last-converge time (for example from the remote-tracking ref's reflog) and classify stale by that time, falling back to oldest-unpushed only when no reflog exists.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify (and test in the shadow/probe stage) a rollback that replays post-swap event files onto the restored backup history before republishing, with its own CAS precondition.
evidence: "Rollback: immutable backup ref `refs/tickets-backup/pre-reclaim-<date>` (or the S3 rollback bundle prefix) before the swap"
"the swap is one revertible step"
findings.finding: The rollback restores `refs/tickets-backup/pre-reclaim-<date>` (or the S3 rollback prefix). It does not address events written onto the NEW baseline after the swap and before rollback. Restoring the backup is itself another non-FF rewrite that discards those writes, or forces clients through a second divergence and replay. So 'one revertible step' is not cheap and not free of data cleanup, and the revert is not stated to be tested.
scenarios: After the swap, clients reconcile and push new events; verify-authorship then fails and the operator restores the backup ref, losing every post-swap event and forcing all clones to diverge again.
findings.suggested_fix: Define the rollback as: (1) take a CAS snapshot of the current new head; (2) extract event files added since the swap; (3) replay them onto the backup ref; (4) CAS-publish. Exercise this revert path in the S2/probe stage.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify deploy ordering: ship S3 override + replay-reconcile client code first, gate the swap on a minimum client version (or a remote-side marker that old clients refuse), and only then run the reclaim.

findings.finding: The plan depends on client-side behavior: S3 stale-clone forced override on reconnect, and post-swap reconcile by EVENT-FILE REPLAY rather than history merge. An un-upgraded client will do a normal history merge or push, including the S3 auto-doctor lossless merge, and reintroduce the old lineage.

scenarios: The reclaim runs while a teammate's clone still runs a rebar version without replay-reconcile; its next auto-push merges old history back into `tickets`.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a rollout sequence. (1) Release client support for the replay-reconcile and override paths. (2) Publish a rewrite-epoch marker on the remote that the new client honors and that old clients cannot push past (e.g. a version check in sync). (3) Wait for adoption. (4) Run the swap.

findings.finding: Clients synced within N days have no way to tell that history was rewritten, so the reconcile path does not achieve the goal. S3 is described only as 'stale-clone detection + forced remote-override' for clones stale beyond N days, while every other clone is said to 'reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline'. The plan names no signal that switches a recent clone from its normal non-fast-forward fetch+merge sync to replay, and no minimum-version or capability gate for clones running older rebar. Any such clone will merge the rewritten remote with its old local history and auto-push the merge, making all 235K old commits reachable on tickets again. The replay set is also unspecified. It must be the clone's unpushed delta relative to the pre-fetch remote-tracking SHA, not 'append-only files' generally. Otherwise local copies of reclaimed .retired or pre-baseline event files are re-added to the baseline tree.
findings.location: ## Mechanism — S3 / ## Feasibility — 'Clients reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline'
scenarios: A developer's clone, synced 2 days ago and running the previous rebar release, writes a comment; auto-sync merges origin/tickets (rewritten) with local tickets (old history) and pushes the result, undoing the reclaim.
A recent clone that does replay copies every local event file, including reclaimed .retired files, back into the baseline tree.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the published baseline carry a superseding compat epoch plus a required capability. Clients that lack the capability refuse to sync or push. Clients that have it detect remote_epoch_supersedes_local, record the pre-fetch origin/tickets SHA, replay only the event files added in local commits not reachable from that SHA, then hard-reset onto the new tip.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add an 'Alternatives considered' entry that measures or rejects shallow/`--shallow-since`, treeless `--filter=tree:0` (cite docs/clone-guidance.md's 3.4x result), and measurement-scope narrowing (cite verify-identity.yml:31-44) before stating that history rewrite is the only lever.
evidence: Plan: "`git gc`/repack does NOT shrink it (proven). The only lever is reducing reachable commit/tree objects on `tickets` history"
Absence: the plan names no shallow, treeless or refspec-scoping alternative and gives no reason for rejecting them.
Repo prior art: docs/clone-guidance.md:10-11 measured `--filter=tree:0` at 3.57 GiB, 3.4x a full clone. That is a real reason against treeless clones, but the plan does not cite it.

Repo prior art: .github/workflows/verify-identity.yml:31-44 states the 100 MiB limit is 'for the CODE checkout pack, not for the append-only `tickets` event log' and narrows the unshallow refspec so `tickets` is absent at measurement time.
GitHub's partial/shallow-clone guidance describes treeless clones as fetching commits first and trees and blobs on demand, and recommends shallow clones for throwaway CI checkouts.
findings.finding: The plan says reclaiming tickets history is 'the only lever' for the CI pack budget, but it never considers or rejects the standard client-side ways to shrink a CI fetch: shallow or `--shallow-since=<N days>` fetch of `tickets`, treeless `--filter=tree:0`, or narrowing which refspec the budget measures. Choosing a destructive rewrite of every SHA on a shared branch should first show why these cheaper, well-known options do not work.
scenarios: The budget can be met by changing the fetch shape or measurement scope (as verify-identity.yml now does), yet the team still rewrites history on a protected shared branch, forcing every clone to diverge and accepting loss of >N-day work for no gain.

The verify-authorship/op-cert walk needs full tickets history, which would rule out shallow fetch, but the plan does not record that, so reviewers cannot confirm the rewrite is really the only option.
findings.suggested_fix: In ## Why, replace 'The only lever is…' with a short table of alternatives: (a) `--shallow-since=30.days` on the tickets fetch: rejected/accepted because verify-identity/op-cert needs full tickets ancestry (cite the exact consumer); (b) `--filter=tree:0`: rejected, measured 3.4x larger due to on-demand tree fetch (docs/clone-guidance.md); (c) scoping the 100 MiB budget to the code checkout only: state whether this already resolves defensive-buckskin-rhino (see verify-identity.yml:31-44) and, if so, re-justify the reclaim on other grounds (clone cost, growth) or narrow its urgency.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Cite tombstone grace-period GC (Cassandra gc_grace_seconds + replace-after-grace) as prior art for C2/C3, and adopt its rule: set N greater than max expected clone offline time plus the reclaim/sync interval, and block any stale clone before its first push.
evidence: Plan: "(C2) that fold reachable on the sync remote's `tickets` ref ≥ N days, (C3) stale clones (>N days) forced to reset to remote"; "residual loss of a >N-day-drifted clone's divergent work is ACCEPTED"
Apache Cassandra docs: a node 'down or disconnected for longer than gc_grace_seconds' has its deleted data 'repaired back to the other nodes' and it reappears.
DataStax docs: a node down longer than the grace period requires removing its data and a node replacement to avoid inconsistency, which matches the plan's C3 forced reset.
AxonOps docs give the rule that gc_grace_seconds must exceed maximum expected node downtime plus repair interval. The plan's N=30d has no stated relation to max clone offline time or sync cadence.
Absence: no external prior art (tombstone grace-period GC, CRDT causal-stability log compaction) is cited for the horizon/override design.
findings.finding: The plan's core idea (garbage-collect tombstones/history after a fixed time horizon, and force any replica offline longer than that to discard its state and resync, accepting its divergent writes as lost) is the well-established Cassandra `gc_grace_seconds` + replace-node-after-grace pattern. The plan presents C1–C5 as a new 'causal-stability' proof without citing this prior art or adopting its documented rules: the horizon must exceed max expected downtime plus the anti-entropy/sync interval, and returning replicas must be detected and blocked before they can push.
scenarios: A clone offline for just under N days with unpushed writes comes back during or right after a reclaim. Without a margin for sync/reclaim cadence (Cassandra's 'downtime + repair interval'), the boundary case behaves differently from what the proof assumes.

S3 stale-clone detection is enforced only 'on reconnect'. Cassandra's experience shows zombie resurrection happens when a stale replica rejoins before detection, so the order of detection versus the first push matters.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a 'Prior art' paragraph to the DESIGN + PROOF mapping C2 to gc_grace_seconds and C3 to Cassandra's mandatory replace/wipe of a node down longer than the grace period. Then add to S1/S3: (a) N must exceed the documented max clone-offline expectation plus the reclaim cadence; (b) the S3 stale check runs before any push/sync from a clone, not after.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a child slice (and a pre-swap gate) that implements and deploys event-file-replay reconciliation for clones newer than N days, including those with unpushed writes. It should detect that the remote was rewritten, refuse history-merge or force-push of old ancestry, and replay local-only event files onto the new baseline. Require a minimum client version across all clones/worktrees before the swap is allowed.
evidence: "Clients reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline (append-only files, not history merge)"
S3 is scoped only to "stale-clone detection + forced remote-override on reconnect" (>N days).
"A rewrite changes every commit SHA ⇒ every clone/worktree diverges (non-FF update of a shared auto-pushed branch)"
No slice or AC requires the replay client to be deployed to every clone/worktree before the swap.
findings.finding: The plan relies on clones newer than N days (including ones with unpushed writes) reconciling after the swap by 'EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline', and its proof AC depends on that. But replay-onto-a-rewritten-baseline is new client behavior, and no deferred child slice owns it. S3 covers only stale (>N-day) clone detection and forced override. Without that behavior shipped to every clone before the swap, a recent clone's existing auto-sync would either fail on the non-fast-forward or reconcile by history merge. A history merge pulls the whole old history (and retired events) back onto `tickets` on its next auto-push, undoing the reclaim and losing writes made after the cutover.
findings.location: Feasibility → 'Clients reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY'; Deferred child-slice work S0–S3
scenarios: A 2-day-old clone with unpushed events auto-pushes after the swap. Its sync merges its old-history parent with the new baseline, pushes the merge, and all reclaimed commits/trees become reachable again.
A worktree running an older rebar version keeps hitting non-fast-forward rejections and its writes stall.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the replay-reconcile behavior to S3 (or a new S2.5), with a remote-side marker (e.g. a reclaim-generation ref or note pointing at the baseline) that clients check before syncing, and have the server/CAS reject any push whose ancestry contains the pre-reclaim tip.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State where the pre-reclaim backup lives (on the sync remote and, ideally, as an offsite bundle file), how it is protected from deletion or force-update (protected-ref rule / S3 object-lock), confirm that it is not fetched by the blobless CI checkout, and add a pre-swap check that the backup is readable from a separate machine.
evidence: "immutable backup ref `refs/tickets-backup/pre-reclaim-<date>` (or the S3 rollback bundle prefix) before the swap"
"Offline reclamation in a disposable clone (I9b isolation)"
findings.finding: The backup's storage location and durability are not specified. It isn't clear whether `refs/tickets-backup/pre-reclaim-<date>` is created on the sync remote (GitHub/Gerrit/bare) or only in the disposable reclaim clone, which is thrown away by design. Git refs are also not 'immutable' by default. If the backup exists only in the disposable clone, or can be deleted or force-updated on the remote (or pruned by server-side GC), rollback after an approved one-way swap becomes impossible. If it is pushed to the remote, the plan should confirm that this ref is excluded from the blobless CI checkout so it doesn't cancel the pack win.
scenarios: The backup ref is written only in the disposable clone, the clone is cleaned up, and a defect found days later has no restore point.
The backup ref on GitHub is deleted by a branch-cleanup rule or force-updated by a mistaken push.
findings.suggested_fix: Push the backup ref to the remote under a protected namespace and also write a `git bundle` of the pre-reclaim tip to durable storage, using object-lock where available. Gate the swap on verifying that the backup can be fetched or reread from outside the disposable clone.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that the disposable reclaim clone is a full (no --filter) clone, or a partial clone with an explicit blob prefetch, and add a preflight that asserts no promisor remote/partial-clone filter before S2 runs
evidence: Plan: "235,482 commits, 408,295 trees, ZERO blobs blobless"
Plan: "Offline reclamation in a disposable clone ..., never interactive"
Plan S2: "coalesce to a re-signed baseline checkpoint = compacted as-of-horizon state + carried authorship_ledger"
Evidence class: Unverified (clone mode for the disposable clone is not specified)
findings.finding: The plan says the guarded checkout is blobless ('ZERO blobs blobless') and that reclamation runs 'offline' in a disposable clone. It never says that clone must be a full (non-partial) clone. S2 must materialize the compacted as-of-horizon state and re-sign the SNAPSHOT/authorship_ledger, which needs blob contents. Run in a blobless partial clone, fast-export/fast-import or mktree (which checks objects exist unless --missing is passed) will lazily fetch promisor objects over the network, or fail when offline.
findings.location: Mechanism — 'Offline reclamation in a disposable clone (I9b isolation)'; S2
scenarios: An operator clones with --filter=blob:none, as CI does; the coalesce triggers hundreds of thousands of lazy blob fetches or fails when network access is restricted
findings.suggested_fix: In S2's preflight, assert `git config --get remote.<name>.promisor` and `extensions.partialClone` are unset (that is, a full clone) before any fast-import/mktree step; document the expected clone size.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the client-side gate (minimum rebar version / superseding store-epoch capability honoured by the S3 auto-doctor and sync) that must be deployed to all clients before the S3 swap, so no client's doctor folds a pre-baseline head back in
evidence: Plan: "its non-interactive auto-doctor ... NEVER discards a head, so a normally-pushed rewrite would be MERGED BACK (resurrected)"
Plan: "Clients reconcile post-swap by EVENT-FILE REPLAY onto the baseline": no rollout ordering or version gate is stated
docs/s3-backend.md:139-145: the doctor runs automatically on any client's push when more than one bundle exists
Evidence class: Partially-verified (doctor behaviour verified in s3_doctor.py; client-side gating is not specified in the plan)
findings.finding: The plan bypasses the auto-doctor only on the publisher side. The doctor still runs on every other client and folds any multi-bundle state by lossless merge, never dropping a head. After the swap, a pre-swap-based client, or one on an older rebar without the stale-clone override, can produce a second bundle whose head descends from the old history. That client's doctor would then merge the rewritten-away history back in. The plan does not say how other clients' doctors are stopped from folding pre-baseline heads, e.g. a minimum rebar version or store-epoch capability gate that clients must honour before the S3 swap.
findings.location: Feasibility — adapter (b) 'deliberately BYPASSING the auto-doctor'; S3 stale-clone override
scenarios: A <N-day clone on an older rebar pushes concurrently right after the swap; two bundles exist; its doctor merges the old tip with the baseline, and the old commit/tree history is reachable again

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Define the post-rollback state and its checks. Revert enforce_since (rebar.toml / REBAR_IDENTITY_ENFORCE_SINCE) together with the tickets ref, replay post-swap event files onto the restored history (compensating forward, not a blind reset), restore the ledger annotations, and require `rebar fsck` + full-log replay + verify-authorship to be green on the restored graph. Attach a DATA LOSS RISK note for writes made after the swap.
evidence: "Rollback: immutable backup ref `refs/tickets-backup/pre-reclaim-<date>` ... the swap is one revertible step"
"re-anchor `enforce_since` to the baseline" — enforce_since is configured in rebar.toml:151 (`enforce_since = "f9f38d0c..."`), separate from the tickets ref
"re-resolves `position→commit_sha` in the NEW graph, rewrites the SNAPSHOT ledger annotations"
No post-rollback assertions: no requirement that verify-authorship and fsck pass on the restored graph, and no rule for writes made after the swap.
findings.finding: Rollback is called 'one revertible step', but the plan never states what persisted state looks like afterwards. Restoring `tickets` to refs/tickets-backup/pre-reclaim-<date> leaves three problems. (i) `identity.enforce_since`, which lives in rebar.toml on the code branch (rebar.toml:151), still points at the rewritten baseline, a commit that is no longer an ancestor of the restored tip, so verify_authorship's ancestry era-check misclassifies every event. (ii) Any SNAPSHOT ledger `commit_sha` annotations re-resolved against the new graph are invalid. (iii) Events that clients wrote and pushed on top of the new baseline after the swap are dropped from `tickets`. The plan has no compensating-forward step (replaying post-swap event files onto the restored history) and no coordinated revert of rebar.toml. DATA LOSS RISK: events written after the swap and before the rollback are lost unless they are explicitly replayed.
scenarios: The swap is published, clients reconcile and push 2 hours of events onto the new baseline, a defect is found, and the operator resets `tickets` to the backup ref. Those 2 hours of events vanish, and verify-identity fails because enforce_since is not an ancestor of the restored tip.
rebar.toml's enforce_since change is merged on main before the swap. When the swap is rolled back, the merge gate starts failing on every PR.
findings.suggested_fix: Make rollback a scripted procedure rather than a ref reset: (1) CAS-restore `tickets` to the backup ref plus a replay of every event file added since the baseline, (2) revert enforce_since in the same coordinated change, (3) have clients re-run replay-reconcile against the restored tip, (4) assert that fsck, replay, and verify-authorship are clean and that the event-file count is at least the pre-rollback count before declaring rollback done.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Amend ADR 0106 (C4/proof) to cover re-signing and author_id back-fill as an operator-approved exception, and teach reclaim_dry_run a `resign` mode so the go/no-go evidence comes from the tested harness.
evidence: Parent Design: 'Under C1–C5: no still-observable state changes, no signature verification breaks'.
f04e: 'give the 253 events `author_id` 594c'; AC: 'reduced state ... equals the original apart from `authorship` counts and the added `author_id`s'.
f04e: '`reclaim_dry_run.py` is unchanged (its equality checks assume a verdict-preserving collapse); the real-data proof uses an out-of-repo driver'.
8dc4: 'The reclaim must not change any event's verdict ... this is a comparison, not an exit-0 check.'
findings.finding: f04e changes still-observable ticket state and verdicts during the reclaim. It re-signs failing events with a bot key and adds `author_id` to 253 events. That contradicts the parent's proof claim 'Under C1–C5: no still-observable state changes' and 8dc4's verdict-preserving equality checks. To get around this, f04e moves the real-data proof to an out-of-repo driver, so the history evidence used for the production swap comes from no tested in-repo harness.
scenarios: The production swap publishes a history in which previously unsigned or foreign-key events now carry a bot signature attributed to identity 594c. The ADR 0106 proof (C4 carriage or grandfathering) does not describe this, and 8dc4's go/no-go packet did not exercise it.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a `--resign-plan` path to reclaim_dry_run with expected verdict deltas (failures→verified) in place of strict equality, and record the attestation-semantics change in ADR 0106 §4.

evidence: "Max safe win N=30d ≈ 365–380 MiB; N=7d ≈ 200–215 MiB; ≤100 MiB needs an unsafe <4-day horizon."
"the blobless CI checkout pack is ~481 MiB vs a deliberate 100 MiB budget"

metrics.claim_path: no-llm/no-network (structural; the fast claim check is a local HMAC verify)
